extracted.intended_audience: judges, litigators, law students, and IP practitioners concerned with fee-shifting under 35 U.S.C. § 285
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and interpretive standards for when a court may award reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party in a patent infringement case under 35 U.S.C. § 285, including competing tests (Brooks two-part test vs. totality-of-the-circumstances) and related doctrines. The page summarizes factual background, arguments, precedent, and policy considerations bearing on whether a case is "exceptional."

rubrics_metrics.name: Brooks two-part test (objective baselessness + subjective bad faith)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Federal Circuit's Brooks-derived rule, an accused infringer may recover attorney fees under § 285 only if the patent-holder's claim was (1) objectively baseless and (2) brought in subjective bad faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts applying Brooks require the accused infringer to prove both elements (objective baselessness and subjective bad faith), typically by clear and convincing evidence. The Federal Circuit has applied this as a restrictive standard that limits fee awards absent a showing of bad faith. Icon defends this two-prong test as consistent with precedent and congressional intent; Octane argues it is too narrow and not party-neutral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the-circumstances discretionary standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court may exercise equitable discretion and consider the totality of the circumstances to determine whether a case is "exceptional" and therefore merits an award of attorney fees under § 285.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents (including Octane and the United States) urge a totality approach that considers multiple non-exhaustive factors—such as reasonableness of the claim, choice of venue, and predatory patent litigation (including PAE activity)—similar to fee standards in other IP areas (copyright, trademark). The Court could therefore vacate Brooks and endorse broad district-court discretion rather than a rigid two-part test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct-based exceptionality (fraud, litigation misconduct, Rule 11 violations, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: A case may be deemed "exceptional" under § 285 based on patent or litigation misconduct without needing to satisfy the Brooks two-part test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Icon and courts recognize that fraud, inequitable conduct before the PTO, litigation misconduct, willful infringement, Rule 11 violations, and similar infractions may independently render a case exceptional and justify fee shifting. The Brooks two-prong test is said to apply only where such misconduct is not shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for exceptionality (clear and convincing evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may require that the party seeking fees prove exceptionality by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the district court here, Octane failed to establish by clear and convincing evidence either element of the two-prong test. Parties dispute whether that heightened proof requirement should control in all § 285 proceedings, but it is the standard applied by some courts when evaluating bad faith/objective baselessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity principle between prevailing plaintiffs and defendants (Fogerty analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: For fee-shifting provisions, the same standard should apply to prevailing plaintiffs and prevailing defendants; courts should not impose a higher hurdle on defendants seeking fees than on plaintiffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Octane invokes Fogerty (copyright fee-shifting) to argue courts should not treat accused infringers less favorably than patentees. This principle supports rejecting a defendant-disadvantaging two-prong rule and adopting a neutral, discretionary standard. Icon disputes direct application of Fogerty, noting textual differences in statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual and statutory-construction cues ('may' and 'exceptional' imply discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory text of § 285—specifically the use of the permissive 'may' and the modifier 'exceptional'—suggests district courts possess broad discretion to award fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Octane argues that the ordinary meaning of the statute supports equitable discretion and a totality-of-the-circumstances approach; interpreting § 285 so narrowly as to duplicate inherent authority would render the statute superfluous, which statutory-construction principles disfavour. Icon argues congressional intent and historical practice counsel restraint to avoid chilling meritorious claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative statutory interpretation (limits of importing other IP fee standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons to fee-shifting provisions in other IP statutes (e.g., Copyright Act §505; Lanham Act §1117(a)) are informative but have limits based on textual differences and circuit splits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The United States and Octane point to Fogerty and Noxell as support for broader discretion; Icon counters that §285's explicit 'exceptional' language distinguishes it from §505 and that courts are divided about applying Lanham Act approaches, so cross-statute analogies are persuasive but not dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of patent assertion entities (PAEs) and predatory litigation as relevant factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a plaintiff is a PAE or engages in conduct characteristic of 'patent trolls' (acquiring patents to demand settlements rather than to practice an invention) can be a relevant factor in assessing exceptionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amicus briefs (e.g., Apple) urge the Court to allow district courts to consider PAE behavior and predatory litigation tactics under a totality test to discourage frivolous suits. Icon resists tailoring § 285 to address PAEs, arguing Congress should act if a different rule is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding chilling of legitimate claims and First Amendment petition concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Any standard for awarding fees must take into account policy concerns that a looser standard could deter bona fide patent holders from exercising their right to petition the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Icon argues that a generous fee-shifting regime could chill First Amendment petitioning and legitimate enforcement of patent rights; courts should balance deterrence of frivolous suits with protection of valid claims when deciding whether a case is "exceptional."

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding interpretive redundancy (§285 should have independent effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretations of § 285 should not render the statute superfluous by collapsing its operation into courts' existing inherent authority to sanction misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Octane argues that if § 285 merely duplicates inherent powers (e.g., sanctions for litigation misconduct), Congress's grant of authority via § 285 would be pointless; therefore, § 285 should be construed to provide an independent, discretionary basis for fee awards beyond established sanctions.
